question: On a dataset with 95% negatives, a model that always predicts negative has what accuracy?
explanation: It is right on every negative, which is 95% of the data, while catching zero positives. This is why accuracy misleads on imbalanced data.

question: Which metric answers the question: of all the items the model flagged as positive, what fraction were actually positive?
explanation: Precision = TP / (TP + FP), the fraction of positive predictions that were correct.

question: You lower the classification threshold from 0.8 to 0.3. What typically happens?
options: Neither changes because the model is the same
explanation: A lower threshold flags more items: more true positives (higher recall) but also more false positives (usually lower precision).

question: A model has ROC AUC = 0.9. What does that mean?
options: A randomly chosen positive gets a higher score than a randomly chosen negative 90% of the time
explanation: ROC AUC measures ranking quality: the probability that a random positive outranks a random negative. It does not depend on any threshold.

question: With 0.5% positives, why is average precision often more informative than ROC AUC?
options: ROC AUC cannot be computed with imbalanced data
The false positive rate stays tiny even with many false positives because negatives are so numerous, so ROC AUC can look excellent while precision is poor
Average precision is always higher than ROC AUC
explanation: FPR divides false positives by a huge number of negatives, hiding them. Precision divides by the number of flagged items, so it exposes a flood of false alarms.

question: A regression model has MAE = 10 and RMSE = 40. What does the gap suggest?
options: A few very large errors dominate the squared error
The model always predicts the mean
RMSE was computed incorrectly; it cannot exceed MAE
explanation: RMSE squares errors before averaging, so a handful of large errors inflate it far more than MAE. RMSE is always at least MAE.
